books.section: Topic 4.7 Expanding Democracy, A. Participatory Democracy and an Expanding Electorate
The Whig Party and the Second Party System

stimulus.text: The lithograph shows General William Henry Harrison in military uniform, with a wreath below naming him “of Tippecanoe, Fort Meigs and the Thames.” Published in 1840. In that year the Whigs nominated Harrison, a hero of the War of 1812, for president. After a colorful campaign, which included the catchy slogan “Tippecanoe and Tyler Too,” Harrison was elected. He died a month after taking office, and Vice President John Tyler became the first vice president to succeed to office after the death of a president. (Paraphrase of 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 13.)
stimulus.source_note: Lithograph “General Wm. H. Harrison of Tippecanoe, Fort Meigs and the Thames,” published 1840 (Library of Congress). Public domain; text paraphrases 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 13. Viewed before writing.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The lithograph presents Harrison mainly as

options.text: a military hero of Tippecanoe, Fort Meigs, and the Thames
a frontier farmer in a log cabin
options.misconception: No cabin appears; Harrison wears a general's uniform and the wreath names his battles.

options.text: a president of the Bank of the United States
options.misconception: Harrison never ran the Bank; the Whigs backed the Bank, but the portrait sells the soldier.
Nothing in the portrait suggests preaching; it shows a uniformed general.

rationales.A: The uniform, the sword, and the wreath naming Tippecanoe, Fort Meigs, and the Thames all sell Harrison the soldier.
rationales.B: The portrait shows a uniformed general, not a farmer in a cabin.
rationales.C: Harrison never led the Bank; the portrait sells the soldier.
rationales.D: The portrait shows a general, not a preacher.
rationales.general:
1. Read the uniform. Harrison wears a general's dress uniform with epaulettes and a sword.
2. Read the wreath. It names his three battles: Tippecanoe, Fort Meigs, and the Thames.
3. Read the year. The portrait was published in 1840, his campaign year, to sell the hero.
Background: Harrison was a hero of the War of 1812, and the Whigs made his battles the center of his campaign.
Remember: a campaign portrait is an advertisement, so ask what it is selling.
